title: Least effort trail
prompt:
A hiker crosses a map of heights, starting at the top-left cell and finishing at the bottom-right cell. Each move goes one cell up, down, left or right. The strain of a move is the absolute difference between the two heights, and the effort of a whole trail is its largest single strain. Return the smallest effort of any trail from start to finish.

- heights has 1 to 100 rows and 1 to 100 columns; every row has the same length.
- 0 <= heights[r][c] <= 1,000,000.
hints: Treat each cell as a node and each move as an edge whose weight is the strain. The cost of a path is the maximum weight on it, not the sum.
Dijkstra still works when a path's cost is max(effort so far, next strain): extending a path never makes it cheaper.
Return as soon as you pop the bottom-right cell. Its effort is final at that point.

solution.explanation: Run Dijkstra on the grid where the cost of a path is its largest strain. A min-heap holds (effort, row, column). Popping a cell fixes its effort, because any other route to it must pass through a cell with at least that effort. Each neighbour gets max(effort, strain); if that beats its best so far, push it. The first time the goal is popped, its effort is the answer.

complexity.notes: Each cell can be pushed a few times, once per improving neighbour, and every heap operation is O(log(R·C)). An alternative is to binary search the effort and run BFS for each guess, which costs O(R·C·log H) for heights up to H.

followUps: Solve it by binary searching on the effort with a BFS check, then compare the two approaches.
Solve it with Union-Find: add moves in order of strain until the start and finish join.
